{"id": "20:130/q19", "question": "What do reports say about guarding the two prayers before sunrise and sunset?", "turns_on": "These are distinct reports about the same two prayer times, with different promised merits or wording.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q19/p1", "position": "The Prophet likened believers' vision of God to seeing the full moon, then urged guarding the two prayers and cited this verse.", "reasons": "Jarir transmits the report across Yahya, Tabari, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Durr and Bursevi; Ibn Kathir calls it authentic and Biqai says both Sahih collections transmit it."}, {"id": "20:130/q19/p2", "position": "Whoever performs the prayers before sunrise and sunset will not enter the Fire.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites Muslim through Umara ibn Ruwayba; Durr repeats the report."}, {"id": "20:130/q19/p3", "position": "The Prophet called them the two asr prayers and explained them as prayers before sunrise and sunset.", "reasons": "Durr and Alusi transmit the instruction to Fadala ibn Wahb."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q20", "question": "What further reports describe divine vision and reward?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different events or degrees of heavenly reward.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q20/p1", "position": "The highest-ranking person in Paradise sees God twice daily, unlike the lowest rank's thousand-year kingdom.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir transmits a report from Ibn Umar."}, {"id": "20:130/q20/p2", "position": "God asks the people of Paradise if they are content, then grants His abiding pleasure.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir calls the report authentic."}, {"id": "20:130/q20/p3", "position": "The lifting of the veil and vision of God surpass all prior gifts to Paradise's people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports the people recall whitened faces, heavy scales, rescue from Fire and admission to Paradise, then receive the increase of vision."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q21", "question": "What reports or rulings concern prayer practice beyond the fixed times?", "turns_on": "Different reported legal allowances and merits concerning prayer practice.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q21/p1", "position": "Prayers may be combined during travel or rain, and advancing them is preferable.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits al-Shafi'i's view."}, {"id": "20:130/q21/p2", "position": "Prayers may be combined for occupation and a valid excuse.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits al-Hadi's allowance."}, {"id": "20:130/q21/p3", "position": "Combining is allowed generally, while Abu Hanifa distinguishes which prayers may be advanced.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports these further legal approaches without details of Abu Hanifa's distinctions."}, {"id": "20:130/q21/p4", "position": "Isha and Fajr are hardest on hypocrites, though their reward would bring attendance even by crawling.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits the hadith."}, {"id": "20:130/q21/p5", "position": "Keeping the five prayers in congregation brings broad benefits; neglect brings losses.", "reasons": "Bursevi relays a report without enumerating all its benefits or losses in the note."}, {"id": "20:130/q21/p6", "position": "The community receives mercy and calamities are averted through sincerity, prayer, supplication and weak members.", "reasons": "Bursevi transmits this hadith and a report that Daniel ascribed rescue from Noah's flood, Ad's wind and Thamud's blast to prayer like this community's."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q22", "question": "How many prescribed prayers does this verse encompass, and when?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is a fixed prayer timetable, includes extra devotions, or uses tasbih more generally; chronology of five prayers is also disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q22/p1", "position": "It encompasses all five daily prayers.", "reasons": "Qatada's common mapping is Fajr, Asr, Maghrib, Isha and Dhuhr; Ibn Abbas and Razi assign Dhuhr with Asr before sunset and repeat dawn or sunset at the edges. Razi prefers the five-prayer interpretation among prayer readings; Ibn Ashur relies on mass-transmitted practice. Islahi says the verse rebuts claims that prayer times are absent from the Qur'an, while the Prophet defines each prayer's extent."}, {"id": "20:130/q22/p2", "position": "It names four fixed prayers and omits noon.", "reasons": "Razi reports the four-prayer interpretation; Tabatabai compares the four-prayer pattern of 11:114 and argues both suras predate the institution of five after the Ascension, citing 17:78."}, {"id": "20:130/q22/p3", "position": "It includes five obligatory prayers and also additional voluntary worship in night and day.", "reasons": "Razi reports this second prayer reading; Ibn Atiyya and Biqai allow voluntary rites. Islahi specifies tahajjud and ishraq and says extra worship should be maintained in collective or individual hardship."}, {"id": "20:130/q22/p4", "position": "It primarily urges continuous glorification rather than legislating a count of obligatory prayers.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the lexicon does not require prescribed prayer; Kur'an Yolu argues five were not yet obligatory in the sura's period and takes thought, word and deed as means of peace."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q23", "question": "What was the historical sequence of obligatory prayer?", "turns_on": "How the verse's date relates to the development of the five obligatory prayers.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q23/p1", "position": "Prayer began as two cycles at dawn and evening; after the Ascension five two-cycle prayers except sunset were imposed, then completed after migration.", "reasons": "Muqatil reports the sequence."}, {"id": "20:130/q23/p2", "position": "This command predates the obligation of five prayers.", "reasons": "Durr transmits al-Suddi; Tabatabai dates Ta-Ha and Hud before the post-Ascension al-Isra and suggests four daily prayers then, with five later at 17:78. Kur'an Yolu also uses the earlier date against a five-prayer reading."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q24", "question": "How does this verse connect to its immediate context and other verses?", "turns_on": "The sources connect different clauses to prior delay, prayer parallels and later promises.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q24/p1", "position": "The fixed but delayed judgment in 20:129 grounds patience in 20:130, followed by worship rather than preoccupation with worldly comfort.", "reasons": "Tabari and Ibn Ashur explain the prior decree and term; Qashani invokes 8:33 and the Prophet's mercy to explain why the community is spared; Bursevi and Alusi call delay respite. Ibn Ashur and Islahi connect patience and prayer to the warning against coveting comforts and to the God-fearing outcome; Kur'an Yolu reads the sura's end as encouragement under pressure."}, {"id": "20:130/q24/p2", "position": "The command recalls seeking help through patience and prayer in 2:45 and 2:153.", "reasons": "Razi and Alusi explicitly compare those verses; Tabatabai compares them when explaining contentment with decree."}, {"id": "20:130/q24/p3", "position": "The day-end expressions and repeated prayers are clarified by 11:114, 2:238 and related prayer-time verses.", "reasons": "Farra, Kashshaf, Razi, Ibn Ashur, Tabatabai and Asad invoke Hud 11:114 or the middle prayer in 2:238; Bursevi notes parallel discussions at Hud and Qaf."}, {"id": "20:130/q24/p4", "position": "The promised contentment recalls 93:5, with some readings also compared with 19:55 or the high station of 17:79.", "reasons": "Farisi, Wahidi, Baghawi, Razi, Ibn Kathir, Bursevi and Islahi invoke these promises and prophetic descriptions in arguing over reward, intercession and passive reading."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q25", "question": "Was verse 20:130 revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Reports of exceptions to the sura's Meccan classification versus the local style and context.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q25/p1", "position": "It belongs with the generally Meccan sura.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports the majority classify all of Ta-Ha as Meccan; Kur'an Yolu doubts the Medinan reports because the style is Meccan; Study Quran says context supports Mecca."}, {"id": "20:130/q25/p2", "position": "Verses 20:130–131 are Medinan exceptions to the Meccan sura.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports al-Sakhawi's exception for 20:130 and possible 20:131; Study Quran notes this classification."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q26", "question": "What other transmitted facts are given about Sūrat Ṭā Hā?", "turns_on": "The notes transmit distinct names, a virtue report, and an occasion for the following verse.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q26/p1", "position": "It is named Ṭā Hā from its opening letters; the name appears in the account of Umar's conversion.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the written letter forms, rather than pronounced names, supply the title, as with al-Araf; he notes the Sunna conversion account."}, {"id": "20:130/q26/p2", "position": "It is also called Sūrat al-Kalīm.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports al-Sakhawi."}, {"id": "20:130/q26/p3", "position": "It is also called Sūrat Mūsā.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur reports al-Hudhali's Complete."}, {"id": "20:130/q26/p4", "position": "A report says God recited it two thousand years before creating heaven and earth, and angels rejoiced for its recipient community.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites Abu Hurayra in al-Darimi; Ibn Furak explains the report as God making His speech audible to selected angels."}, {"id": "20:130/q26/p5", "position": "A reported Medinan exception at the following verse is tied to a Jewish lender's demand for collateral.", "reasons": "Itqan cites Abu Rafi's account of a flour loan and the Prophet's assertion of trustworthiness before the revelation forbidding coveting worldly provision."}]}

{"id": "20:130/q28", "question": "What ancillary articulation accounts bear on accurate recitation?", "turns_on": "How subsidiary sounds and neighboring points are grouped for a numerical inventory.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q28/p1", "position": "Arabic has twenty-nine basic letters, with additional accepted sounds and disfavored variants; its sounds have detailed articulation and acoustic classes.", "reasons": "Sibawayh counts thirty-five with accepted subsidiaries and forty-two including rare sounds excluded from Qur'an and poetry; he locates sixteen points, distinguishes nineteen voiced and ten whispered letters, explains nasalization, stop and fricative classes, and four emphatics. Direct oral transmission teaches the distinctions; his weak dad may use either tongue side."}, {"id": "20:130/q28/p2", "position": "The articulation points are commonly counted as sixteen, with specific throat, tongue, teeth, lip and nasal locations.", "reasons": "Itqan reports the sixteen-point school and the reciters' test using a prefixed hamzat al-wasl and still or doubled consonant; it assigns long vowels to oral cavity, throat letters in three stages, qaf and kaf to rear tongue, jim-shin-ya to middle tongue, dad to tongue edge by molars, lam-nun-ra to successive tongue positions, dental and sibilant groups to incisor contacts, labials to lips and ghunna to nasal cavity. Nashr supplies parallel dental, sibilant, interdental, labial and nasal descriptions."}, {"id": "20:130/q28/p3", "position": "Fourteen points suffice when lam, nun and ra are grouped.", "reasons": "Itqan reports another group's alternative count."}, {"id": "20:130/q28/p4", "position": "Each letter has its own point, so numerical groupings are approximations.", "reasons": "Itqan transmits Ibn al-Hajib's qualification."}, {"id": "20:130/q28/p5", "position": "Some derived sounds are counted separately, while others treat them as one easing phenomenon.", "reasons": "Nashr says Sibawayh counts between-between hamza once, whereas others count its alif, waw and ya realizations; imala and tafkhim branch from upright alif and strong imala approaches ya."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q29", "question": "Does confusing ḍād and ẓāʾ invalidate prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q29/p1", "position": "No; the letters are sufficiently similar and the distinction is difficult, so it is not an obligation.", "reasons": "Razi prefers this ruling: both share voicing, frication and emphatic quality; softened dad approaches za. {"id": "20:130/q31", "question": "What general grammatical observations appear in the cited exception examples?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q31/p1", "position": "A fronted exception may be accusative; the regular following exception can be a nominative or genitive badal.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports Khalil's reordered analysis, cites Ka'b ibn Malik's trusted poetic usage, and says an already occupied governor permits nominative or genitive after the exception. {"id": "20:130/q32", "question": "What rhetorical examples accompany the cited discussion?", "turns_on": "The cited examples illustrate different rhetorical mechanisms.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q32/p1", "position": "Poetry can assign an invented cause to a real event or imaginatively transform a comparison.", "reasons": "Jurjani uses the cloud's rain as sweat, fragrance bestowed by the buried, and the yellow sunset attributed to fear of parting; he notes attributions to al-Shibli and Abu al-Ba's. Al-Suli's wind actually blows a cloak but receives jealousy as a fictional motive, while Ibn Wahb invents time's hostility and its loving cause."}, {"id": "20:130/q32/p2", "position": "A layered comparison can approach metaphor when restoring an explicit simile would disrupt syntax or contradict its details.", "reasons": "Jurjani illustrates this with separation's sunset, estrangement's lunar eclipse and examples in which a hero is placed beyond a lion or death; cloud and sea images share the paradox."}, {"id": "20:130/q32/p3", "position": "A sentence's full image may emerge only at its final word, while independent coordinated comparisons remain separate.", "reasons": "Jurjani uses al-Farazdaq's final hajaiya, al-Qatami's dhi al-ghulla, and contrastive fragrance-face-fingertip clauses; he introduces Bashshar and Imru al-Qays for extended compositional similes."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q33", "question": "What further report and grammatical examples are transmitted in ancillary excerpts?", "turns_on": "These are separate ancillary reports and grammatical illustrations in the supplied notes.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q33/p1", "position": "Khadija reassured the Prophet at first revelation by invoking his care for kin.", "reasons": "Burhan transmits her statement."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p2", "position": "Three people trapped in a cave prayed through their best deeds for release.", "reasons": "Burhan transmits their counsel."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p3", "position": "A hadith's use of laysa can negate an entire genus of prayer.", "reasons": "Burhan reports Ibn Malik's grammatical argument from the wording no prayer is more burdensome."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p4", "position": "Relative mā is more ambiguous than alladhī and can refer even to the nonexistent.", "reasons": "Burhan reports al-Suhayli's rejection of equating the two relatives."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p5", "position": "One excerpt exhorts beautifying Qur'an recitation with one's voice.", "reasons": "Razi gives no attribution, chain or grading in the cited excerpt."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p6", "position": "Hamza spellings and pause forms elsewhere illustrate the range of codex-conditioned readings.", "reasons": "Nashr lists ten final fatḥa-preceded hamzas with damma written as waw across several suras; open final hamza after alif permits long, short, sometimes medium substitution and between-between, with further variants for kasra and damma."}, {"id": "20:130/q33/p7", "position": "Hamza and adjacent recitation examples elsewhere include kasra or fatḥa on alif, with kasra preferred in recitation.", "reasons": "Farra reports Hamza's reading of wa-idbar al-sujud at 50:40, a cross-verse illustration."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q34", "question": "Can the day edges repeat the dawn and afternoon prayers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q34/p1", "position": "Yes, if daytime starts at dawn; if it starts at sunrise, the two ends are not parallel.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this alternative to repeating dawn and sunset."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q35", "question": "What is the wording of the vision report's crowding expression?", "turns_on": "The report's different mīm readings yield crowding or injustice as the relevant meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q35/p1", "position": "With doubled mīm, it means viewers will not crowd one another to see God.", "reasons": "Bursevi derives the form from mutual crowding and says a tāʾ is omitted."}, {"id": "20:130/q35/p2", "position": "With light mīm, it means no one is wrongfully excluded from the vision.", "reasons": "Bursevi derives the alternate form from injustice and says all share the vision equally."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q36", "question": "How do the sunrise and sunset phrases function syntactically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q36/p1", "position": "They are temporal modifiers of the command to glorify God.", "reasons": "Tabatabai explicitly makes both phrases modify the preceding imperative."}]}

{"id": "20:131/q04", "question": "What are the things God gave them to enjoy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q04/p1", "position": "Worldly goods and pleasures, especially the wealth of affluent people.", "reasons": "Mujāhid names the rich. {"id": "20:131/q05", "question": "What does 'أزواجا منهم' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether azwāj names paired or grouped recipients, their households, or the varieties of goods; Asad broadens the recipients.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q05/p1", "position": "Groups, kinds, or counterparts among the unbelievers.", "reasons": "Māwardī, Jishumī, Rāzī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī derive it from paired resemblance; Ubayy says they resemble one another in turning from right. {"id": "20:131/q06", "question": "How does 'أزواجا' function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether azwāj is the direct object or a ḥāl after the relative clause.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q06/p1", "position": "It is the object of mattaʿnā, with minhum modifying or explaining it.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī calls it the object; Abū Ḥayyān says minhum modifies it; Ālūsī says min is explanatory and the phrase is fronted for emphasis. {"id": "20:131/q07", "question": "What is the 'flower of worldly life'?", "turns_on": "Whether zahrah is the bloom of worldly goods or a plural adjective for those who enjoy them.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q07/p1", "position": "The world's adornment, brightness, freshness, or beautiful bloom.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Suddī, and many commentators gloss adornment. Ibn Qutayba and Wāḥidī's linguists compare tree blossoms; Ṭabrisī gives luminous complexion, radiant suras, and a radiant day. Qurṭubī contrasts the plant flower with ẓuhrah, a star; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes clothing, livestock, gardens, women, children (28:60). Damghānī links 18:46 and 28:60. Bursevī notes a dinar is called a flower for brief freshness; the Prophet in Ibn Kathīr and Durr names earth's blessings worldly bloom."}, {"id": "20:131/q07/p2", "position": "It can describe radiant worldly people, as the plural of zāhir.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī compares the bright faces and finery of the indulgent with the pallor and rough clothes of the devout; Samīn cites the plural patterns fājir/fajarah and bārr/bararah. Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī transmit it; Ālūsī objects that the adjective denotes a stable quality and the circumstantial parse is poor."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q08", "question": "Why call worldly life a flower?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q08/p1", "position": "It dazzles briefly and fades like a plant's blossom.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya stress quick disappearance; the Prophet calls the world sweet and green in Jishumī and Bursevī. Al-Ālūsī rejects restricting the ruling to the Prophet."}, {"id": "20:132/q02/p2", "position": "The command and ruling are particular to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects this claim, including the inference that a general ruling would permit everyone to leave earning."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q03", "question": "Why is the family singled out for prayer?", "turns_on": "The sources variously emphasize example and instruction, the family's special rank, and shared reliance on God.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q03/p1", "position": "The Prophet should guide the people closest to him and exemplify prayer with them.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī compares Ismāʿīl and says leading the family to good and teaching others purifies sincerity; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls family one's exemplary dependents. {"id": "20:132/q04", "question": "What prayer is meant in the command?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording chiefly specifies obligatory prayer or embraces voluntary prayer as well.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q04/p1", "position": "The prescribed prayers, performed and enjoined at their appointed times.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī requires prescribed limits; Rāzī says household members can be reminded at set times. Al-Ālūsī calls obligatory prayer most likely and says perseverance does not require prayer all day and night."}, {"id": "20:132/q04/p2", "position": "Prayer broadly, including voluntary or night prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī allows this in light of reports of ʿUmar's night prayer and the Prophet calling his household amid hardship. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes iṣṭibār figuratively as abundant voluntary prayer and cites 73:1–2 and 17:79."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q05", "question": "What does commanding one's family to pray accomplish?", "turns_on": "Which effect of the prayer command the commentator draws out: moral restraint, aid in hardship, worship, or inward discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q05/p1", "position": "It restrains wrongdoing and protects the family from punishment.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Baghawī say prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing; Biqāʿī cites 29:45. Ibn Kathīr connects saving one's family through prayer to 66:6."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p2", "position": "It gives help through hardship and turns attention from wealth toward worship.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī says prayer helps with hardship and prevents preoccupation with livelihood or wealthy habits. Bursevī directs the poor to prayer rather than gazing at the wealthy; al-Wāsiṭī says the prior warning consoles the poor. Ibn Kathīr and Qushayrī connect prayer with relief and provision; Islahi says vigilant prayer builds perseverance."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p3", "position": "It fulfills the worship God asks for, for the worshipper's benefit.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Abū Muslim cite 51:56–57; Ṭabarī contrasts bodily work with wealth and promises reward. Ibn al-Jawzī-zād juxtaposes God's command to worship with His undertaking to provide."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p4", "position": "In an inward reading, it calls the faculties to divine presence and obedience.", "reasons": "Qāshānī takes the family as spiritual and psychic faculties, and prayer as presence, vigilance, obedience, and response."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q06", "question": "What training of children follows from the family prayer command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q06/p1", "position": "Children should be taught prayer before it is obligatory.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this establishes the habit; Abū Dāwūd's sound-chain raised report orders prayer at seven, discipline for it at ten, and separation of their beds."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q07", "question": "What did the Prophet do at ʿAlī and Fāṭima's door after this command?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on duration and time of visit; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats a duration as the witness's period of observation and notes the setting problem.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q07/p1", "position": "He came for an unspecified number of months and called them to prayer.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says each morning for several months without grading; Rāzī, Qurṭubī, and Bursevī report the morning visits. {"id": "20:132/q08", "question": "What did the Prophet do when hardship struck his household?", "turns_on": "The reports tell either the household-hardship incident, a general resort to prayer in distress, or the distinct servant request.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q08/p1", "position": "He ordered his family to pray and recited this verse.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām versions appear in Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Biqāʿī, Durr, al-Ālūsī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī; Durr grades a chain sound, Biqāʿī quotes al-Ṭabarānī that its chain is singular and Maʿmar alone transmitted it, and al-Ālūsī calls a chain sound. The detail varies between hardship, distress, and tight household provision."}, {"id": "20:132/q08/p2", "position": "The Prophet and earlier prophets resorted to prayer when trouble came.", "reasons": "Thābit generalizes the practice of prophets; Ḥudhayfa says the Prophet resorted to prayer when something troubled him, with Aḥmad transmitting it.
